title: 1675 Mercock Land Dispute
summary: At a hearing on August 5, 1675, Tackapousha and other Native representatives insisted that Hempstead had never paid for Mercock land. Their testimony challenged the town’s evidence and another sachem’s authority to give the land away.

why_this_matters: The 1675 Mercock dispute shows that Native leaders challenged colonial land claims and named unpaid land as an injustice. Dispossession appears here as a contested process involving diplomacy, law, pressure, and resistance.

history_content:
A hearing about land that remained unpaid

On August 5, 1675, Tackapousha and other Native representatives challenged Hempstead’s use of Mercock land before the colonial government. Richard Gildersleeve and George Hewlett appeared for the town. After the Native delegation arrived that afternoon, Tackapousha stated that the land had never been paid for.1

Town representatives invoked a Dutch grant, compensation for livestock, conquest, and a Montaukett sachem’s confirmation. The Native speakers rejected that sachem’s right to give away their land and maintained their claim of nonpayment. When the governor proposed a settlement, they requested time to consult their friends.1

The hearing followed decades of land agreements and boundary negotiations. It exposes the different claims hidden behind the language of purchase: who owned the land, who could consent, what had been paid, and whose account would carry weight. The 1643 deed landscape and Duke’s Laws marker provide the earlier setting for this dispute.123
